tagline.text: A quiet southwestern Cebu town with hot springs, waterfalls, a Spanish watchtower and a coral-stone church

location.label: Location
location.text: Southwestern coast of Cebu Island, a town about 126–139 km south of Cebu City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~2,000 (per person, based on a day trip from Cebu City including transport, fees and meals)

children.text: Malabuyoc is a small coastal town in southwestern Cebu with the Mainit hot springs and waterfalls in Montañeza, a Spanish-era watchtower museum at the heart of town, and the coral-stone church of San Nicolas de Tolentino. It is a quiet place to continue to south of Moalboal.

Malabuyoc is a southwestern coastal town about 126–139 km south of Cebu City (sources differ). The 2024 census counted about 20,000 residents in 14 barangays. It comes right after Alegria, past Moalboal and Badian, a quiet stretch you reach by following the western coastal road down. The name is said to come from "buyok," describing fruit-laden branches bent by their weight. It is one of eight municipalities in Cebu's 7th district and is more a rural town than a tourist destination. So there are no famous resorts or big tours, but the pleasure lies in meeting the springs, hot springs and shore that locals use in daily life. It suits travelers looking for a calm atmosphere in contrast to the busy diving streets of Moalboal.

Historically, the parish separated from Samboan in 1832 and the coral-stone church was completed in 1834. Malabuyoc was reportedly the original municipality from which Alegria and part of Ginatilan were split off. The church is named for San Nicolas de Tolentino, and a festival honoring this patron saint is held around
September 10
every year; since 2004 it has featured the "Binuyokan Festival."

For travelers, Malabuyoc is a nature destination built around water. In Barangay Montañeza there are the Mainit hot springs (four pools of hot water), Montañeza Falls (several small drops and one large drop) and Montañeza Beach, which is good at sunset. Kabutongan Falls in Barangay Looc is known as the most challenging natural site in Malabuyoc, and you must go with a qualified local guide. In the town center there is a museum in a converted Spanish-era watchtower and a coral-stone church, which you can see in an hour or two on foot. The Aranzana Springs, a few hundred meters from the town center, are the source of the water locals drink and wash in, so you can see village life close up. For a one-day plan, put the town (springs, watchtower museum, church) in the morning and Montañeza (beach, hot springs, falls) in the afternoon to cut down on hassle. The Aranzana Springs supply water that residents use, so look around quietly without using soap or shampoo.

Wikipedia also introduces Kanspitan Caves, Da-o Cliff, Balugo Falls, Ilihan Hills, Kagula Cliff and Talangnan Marine Sanctuary. However, some names are not well documented locally, and their locations and access are hard to confirm by search, so it is safer to ask the town tourism office or your lodging owner before going. This guide focuses on the sights that can be confirmed.

This waterfall, less than 1 km from the hot springs, has several small drops and one large one. To reach the last drop you walk a narrow trail, crawl through rock holes, climb carved footholds and wade through knee-deep water. The path may close when it rains.
This small public beach beside the national road has pebbles instead of sand and lovely sunsets. It is better known to locals, so it is quiet.
These freshwater springs a few hundred meters from the town center are the source of the river that locals drink from and wash in. Villagers have built small pools.
This old stone watchtower in the town center was built to protect residents from raiders. It is now used as a museum with local history displays. Check opening hours locally.

blocks.title: Church of San Nicolas de Tolentino

children.text: Built of coral stone, the church has fine bas-relief on its façade and a carved insignia said to show the support of the King of Spain. Seen from above it is cross-shaped, and the bell tower stands out.

These falls in Barangay Looc are challenging, with slippery slopes, waist-deep water, deep pools and climbs over boulders and branches. They are not for beginners, so always go with a qualified local guide.
This shrine, built in the shape of the letter "A," is reached by climbing about 200 concrete steps, and the surroundings suit meditation and relaxation.

items.title: Day route
items.subtitle: Hot springs and a walk through town

children.text: Take a bus bound for Malabuyoc from the Cebu South Bus Terminal in Cebu City.
Arrive in Malabuyoc and look around the watchtower museum and the church in town.
Have an early lunch at a town restaurant.
Move to Montañeza and soak in the Mainit hot springs (they close before sunset).
Relax at Montañeza Beach and enjoy the free time before sunset.
Check the last bus back and return to Cebu City.
The bus ride is long and the last service may stop early, so allow plenty of time or plan to stay a night.
Set out from Moalboal or Badian and head south.
See the town museum and church and leave your bags at your lodging.
Visit the Montañeza hot springs and falls.
Relax at the beach and head home.
Direct flights run daily from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB) and take about
1 hour 30 minutes
. Check airlines and schedules when booking.
From the airport to the Cebu South Bus Terminal in Cebu City takes about
30 minutes to 1 hour
by taxi or Grab.
From the Cebu South Bus Terminal, take a southbound bus on the west-coast route (such as one bound for Bato) and get off at Malabuyoc. It takes about
3–4 hours
. Check the fare locally.
Bus routes change, and buses often drop you at the roadside, such as the Montañeza entrance, so tell the conductor where you want to get off.
Buses on the west-coast road include some that run past Moalboal and Badian as far as Malabuyoc, so you can also transfer in Alegria or stay overnight and continue (check locally).
Follow the coastal road south from Moalboal, Badian or Alegria. A rental car or motorbike makes it easier.
Alegria is the town just before Malabuyoc, so it is worth comparing when choosing lodging.
One review says the Mainit hot springs are about
20 minutes
uphill on foot from a side road. Local motorcycle taxis sometimes take you up.
A guide is not required, but locals may offer to accompany you.
Malabuyoc has the tropical climate of the Cebu west coast. Access paths to the falls and springs get slippery in rain, so the dry season is better.

December to May is the best time to travel, and February to May is hot and dry. June to November is rainy and paths may be closed, but there are fewer people. The hot springs close before sunset, so work out your travel time and arrive early.

If you go in the rainy season, keep in mind that waterfall paths may close; you can still enjoy the trip by switching to the hot springs and the town. Right after rain the stream swells and is dangerous, so follow your guide's judgment.

Travelers usually stay in Alegria, Moalboal or Badian and visit Malabuyoc for half a day to a day. There may also be small lodgings in the town of Malabuyoc, so check booking sites and reviews. Food centers on Cebuano dishes at town restaurants and the market, and no specialty dish has been confirmed.

Stalls may be rare at the springs and waterfalls, so bring water and snacks in advance. Finishing your meal in town before sunset makes the return trip easier. Buying bottled water and snacks in town before heading up to Montañeza is reassuring. In the rainy season, when days are shorter, start early.
The hot springs are said to close before sunset, so arrive early in the afternoon and plan around the last bus.
If you get off the bus at the side-road entrance, the uphill walk is about 20 minutes, so wear comfortable shoes.
At Montañeza Falls you wade through water and crawl over rocks, so bring clothes that can get wet and water shoes.
Bring a waterproof bag or zip bag so your phone and wallet do not get wet at the hot springs and falls.
Kabutongan Falls is hard for beginners and needs a guide.
Dress with your shoulders and knees covered when visiting the church and museum.
Bring plenty of cash. Cards may not work at the hot springs and village shops.
Check in advance the last bus arriving in Malabuyoc and the last bus back.
Plan the hot springs first and the beach afterward, since the beach is best at sunset but the springs close before sunset.
People speak a mix of English and Cebuano, so a translation app makes asking for directions easier.
Reviews say the hot springs have at times been closed or restricted. Check locally before you go whether they are open.
Kabutongan Falls and Montañeza Falls have dangerous stretches and the paths close in rain, so do not go without a guide.
Some sights (Da-o Cliff, Kanspitan Caves and so on) lack access information, so do not push yourself.
Temperatures differ from pool to pool. One review says the hottest pool was about 42℃, so enter slowly, and if you have heart or blood-pressure problems, do not soak for long.
Rural roads after sunset have few streetlights and motorcycles and livestock pass, so avoid traveling at night.
Transport and lodging choices are few, so finish a day trip before dark.
Fares and opening hours may come from older sources, and this guide covers what could be confirmed as of 2026. Check the latest announcements.
Moalboal
on the west coast to the north is known for diving and sardine shoals, with a wide choice of lodging and restaurants.
Kawasan Falls
in Badian can be visited on the way north from Malabuyoc.
Dalaguete on the southeastern coast of Cebu has the Osmeña Peak trek starting point and a beach park. It can be combined in the same southern Cebu itinerary.
